text: Selling to a wholesaler, processor, larger trader, or exporter can offer a better or more predictable market than farm-gate sale, but usually requires meeting a minimum volume, quality standard, moisture level, grade, or delivery schedule that an individual smallholder plot may not produce alone. A higher quoted price does NOT automatically mean higher profit -- once transport, sacks, loading, grading, and losses to a distant buyer are subtracted, a farm-gate trader's offer can produce a better net return. Aggregating through a farmer group or cooperative can make this channel realistic by combining several farms' production to reach the required volume. Cashew is especially relevant to Preah Vihear as one of Cambodia's main cashew-producing areas, and improved varieties like M23/M21 exist in Cambodia, but do not assume any individual farmer grows them without confirmation. For fresh vegetables, the wholesaler/exporter model is hard to apply without reliable cold storage or rapid transport -- nearby buyers and quick delivery are usually more realistic than imitating a commercial supply chain. Before producing for a larger buyer, farmers should know the buyer's exact requirements (variety, size, moisture, packaging, minimum quantity, delivery date, payment timing) in advance, not discover them after a rejected harvest. During the wet season, road/drying conditions affect transport and quality; during the dry season, heat and water scarcity matter more for fresh produce and livestock. Net price = buyer price minus transport, loading, packaging, grading, fees, and expected losses. Do not invent a current local price, buyer specification, or assumed crop variety.
